newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Berisha, opposition halt Albania offensive.
newsitem.headline: Berisha, opposition halt Albania offensive.

text.p: President Sali Berisha, backed by Albania's opposition parties, tried to end a rebellion in the south of the country on Thursday by agreeing to suspend military activity against armed rebels and offer them an amnesty.

A statement issued by the president and 10 parties after more than five hours of talks also said Berisha would seek a political consensus on replacing Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi, who stepped down last weekend.
Berisha later issued a decree enacting the amnesty for insurgents handing in weapons from 6 a.m. (0500 GMT) on Thursday provided they had commited no crimes.

State television said the Defence Council, which oversees emergency rule introduced last weekend, ordered a simultaneous suspension of military action in southern areas where rebels have seized control of several towns.
But many fighters, heavily armed with weapons seized from army depots, vowed to stay dug in until Berisha quit.

At least 16 people have died in the past week, most of them in the Adriatic port of Vlore, focal point of the protests which first erupted last month by investors who lost their life savings in failed pyramid investment schemes.

International attempts at a political solution intensified. A Council of Europe group was in Tirana and the Dutch foreign minister was due on Friday for the European Union. Also expected were the Danish, Swiss and Polish foreign ministers on behalf of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe.
Italy said it had contingency plans to evacuate its nationals if matters deteriorated, but the U.S. State Department denied it had any such intention.

The statement after the talks at Berisha's offices said participants asked the Defence Council "to order the suspension of offensive military operations in the zones where they had been planned, for 48 hours..."
A simultaneous amnesty would also take effect and Berisha was to "start consultations for the appointment of a new prime minister aiming at the greatest possible consensus."
The political parties, Berisha's Democratic Party and nine opposition groups, "supported the restoration of constitutional order and guaranteeing public order throughout the country."

The Socialists, heirs to the communist party and backbone of the Forum for Democracy opposition alliance, added their signature to the statement but their officials made no comment as they left the meeting.
A top Social Democrat, Paskal Milo, said the talks had achieved nothing as Berisha had yet to agree to a coalition government as demanded by his opponents and Western countries.

State television reported that four top military officers, including the commander of navy forces Edmond Zhupani, had been detained and were being investigated for discipline violations, including failure to protect arms against theft.

In the south, a Reuters photographer in the port of Sarande said insurgents were dug in on hilltops east of the town and had set up increasingly well-built barricades against any advance southward by government troops.

Hundreds of rebels paraded through the streets of Tepelene firing into the air with Kalashnikov rifles seized from an army barracks. Wrecks of cars and army vehicles littered the town centre and huge stocks of dynamite were piled in the barracks.
"We will not return our weapons until Berisha resigns," said one colonel. "The army in southern Albania has gone over to the side of the people."
